readerTitle: Same dish, new chalk: rewriting a specials board
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식당 스페셜 보드, 일정 관리 앱 업그레이드 화면) · 모든 수치와 문구는 설명용
insight: 설득은 내용을 바꾸는 일이 아니라, 이미 사실인 것을 손님이 알아보게 보여주는 일이다. 프레이밍과 사회적 증거는 정직한 사실 위에서만 힘을 낸다.
misconception: 스페셜 보드는 메뉴 이름과 가격만 적으면 충분하다. 손님을 끌려면 '오늘만!', '서두르세요!' 같은 강한 말을 써야 한다.

sources.text: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1981). The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice. Science.
Cialdini, R. (1984). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion (social proof).
식당·앱 장면과 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 식당, 메뉴, 가격($26), '지난 금요일 38테이블' 등 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 문구 변경이 판매를 얼마나 늘리는지에 대한 수치는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.
관련 개념 레슨(MKT-03-01 사회적 증거, MKT-03-06 프레이밍)의 정의·용어와 이 레슨의 피드백 문구가 일치하는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.
앱 사례의 '5명 이상 팀 대부분이 Pro를 선택' 문구는 실제 데이터가 있을 때만 쓸 수 있다는 조건을 카드에 명시했습니다. 소비자 보호 관련 법률 조언은 다루지 않습니다.

cards.title: Same dish, new chalk.
body: The board outside a small bistro reads: *SPECIAL: LAMB SHANK $26.*
The lamb is braised for six hours. Regulars order it every Friday. None of that is on the board. Passers-by see a name and a price, then keep walking.
Today you get the chalk. You'll use two ideas from this unit: **framing** and **social proof**.

image.label: Chalkboard with a bare lamb shank special
image.brief: 식당 입구의 A형 칠판. 'SPECIAL: LAMB SHANK $26'만 덩그러니 적혀 있고, 행인 두 명이 힐끗 보고 지나감. 따뜻한 저녁 조명. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Rewrite the first line.
body: Same dish, same $26 price. Which line goes on the board?

options.text: Lamb shank, slow-braised for six hours, with rosemary mash. $26
options.feedback: **Framing** at work: the price now sits next to what it buys. Every word is true, and the six hours makes $26 feel earned.
Every special is today only, so the urgency says nothing new. Shouting can make a bistro feel like a clearance sale.
A reference price is a frame too, and it can work if it's true. But a discount can hint that the dish didn't sell.

cards.title: The frame tells people what they're paying for.
body: The bare board asked one question: *is $26 a lot for lamb?* The new line asks a different one: *is $26 a fair price for six hours of work?*
That's **framing**: the same facts, arranged so people notice different things. Nothing was invented. The cook already braised it for six hours. The board just stopped hiding it.
Sensory, concrete words do most of the work. *Slow-braised* beats *delicious*, because it's something a customer can picture.

cards.title: Now add a second line.
body: The till shows 38 tables ordered the lamb last Friday. You have room for one more line. Which one?

options.feedback: It's **social proof**, but vague. Every board in town says it, so people skim right past.
Specific **social proof**: a real number from people like the reader. It's checkable, so it feels true.
The rating is for the restaurant, not the dish. Borrowed proof feels thin, and it can mislead.

cards.title: Why a number beats an adjective.
body: **Social proof** works because, when unsure, we look at what others chose. A stranger at the door doesn't know your kitchen. Thirty-eight other tables do.
The proof gets stronger when it's specific, recent and from people like the reader. *Last Friday* feels close. *38 tables* feels counted, not claimed.
Framing and social proof stack. The first line says what the dish is. The second says other people already trusted it.

image.label: Before and after chalkboards side by side
image.brief: 칠판 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽 'LAMB SHANK $26'. 오른쪽 'Lamb shank, slow-braised for six hours, with rosemary mash. $26 / 38 tables ordered this last Friday'. 오른쪽 칠판 앞에 멈춰 선 행인. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The chalk can only promise what the kitchen delivers.
body: Both tools rest on true facts. If the lamb was braised for two hours, or the 38 tables are a guess, the board becomes a lie. Customers who taste the gap don't come back.
Keep the proof fresh. *38 tables last Friday* written in March and still up in June is stale.
And don't stack every trick on one board. A frame, a number and a countdown together start to feel like pressure, not information.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling app's upgrade screen.
body: Your app helps teams book meetings. The free plan covers one calendar. Pro costs $12 a month. Your data shows most teams with five or more people choose Pro.
Which upgrade message fits the same two ideas?

options.feedback: Accurate, like the bare chalkboard. It lists a feature but doesn't frame the problem it solves.

options.text: Stop the "what time works?" email chain. Pro, $12/month. Most teams of 5+ choose it.
options.feedback: **Framing** names the pain the price removes, and true **social proof** shows peers already chose it.

options.text: Upgrade now. Prices go up soon!
options.feedback: Urgency with no real deadline borrows trust you'll need later. It also says nothing about why Pro is worth it.

cards.title: Show what's already true, then show who already chose it.
body: You used **framing** to put the price next to what it buys, and **social proof** to add a specific, true number from real customers. Same dish, same price, a clearer board.
**Try it today:** pick one thing you sell. Write one line on what the price buys, and one true line on who already bought it.
